title: Two special endings: ta marbuta and alif maqsura

bigIdea.text: Two letters live only at the end of a word. Ta marbuta (ة) is a 't' when you read on and an 'h' when you stop. Alif maqsura (ى after a fatha) looks like a ya but is read as a long 'aa'.

proper.text: Ta marbuta ('tied ta', ة; joined: ـة) looks like ه with two dots on top. When you continue, read it as ت with its vowel. When you stop on it, it becomes ه with sukun: 'h'.
The same with tanween: continuing gives '-tan', '-tun' or '-tin'; stopping gives just 'h'. Unlike ـًا, a ـةً does not turn into a long 'aa' when you stop.
Alif maqsura ('shortened alif') is written like a ي without dots (ى) at the end of a word, after a fatha. It is a long 'aa', 2 counts. In this mushaf it often carries a small alif (ىٰ) to show this.

Careful: in this mushaf the final ya is written without dots too. So look at what comes before or on it: after a kasra (and no mark of its own) it is a long 'ii'; with its own vowel it is the consonant 'y'; after a fatha (often as ىٰ) it is the long 'aa' of alif maqsura.
ة is not ه: ه is a real 'h' everywhere, while ة is a 't' unless you stop on it.

memoryHook.text: ة: 't' on the move, 'h' at the stop. ى after a fatha: long 'aa'.

extras.text: A few words that usually end in ة are spelled in the mushaf with an open ت. For Hafs you stop on those with 't', following the spelling.

note.text: You read on to the next word, so the ة is a 't' with its kasra.
ة in the middle of the reading: a 't' joined to the next word.
A one-word ayah: when you stop at its end, the ة becomes 'h'.
Two ta marbutas: the first is a 't' joined to the next word; the last, where you stop, is 'h'.
Alif maqsura with a small alif on it (ىٰ): a long 'aa'.
A one-word ayah ending in alif maqsura (ىٰ): a long 'aa'.
A dotless final ya after a kasra: a long 'ii', not alif maqsura.
A dotless final ya with its own fatha: the consonant 'y'.

drills.prompt: Ta marbuta: say ـةَ ـةُ ـةِ as 'ta, tu, ti' (continuing), then the stop form ـهْ ('h') for each.
Alif maqsura: say بَىٰ and تَىٰ as 'baa' and 'taa', 2 counts each. Then the dotless ya after a kasra: ثِى as 'thii', 2 counts.

tip.text: ه is always 'h'. ة is 't' when you read on, and 'h' only when you stop on it.

questions.q: How do you read ة when you continue to the next word?
explain: Right.
'h' is only for stopping.
It is always pronounced.
It is a consonant, not a long vowel.

questions.q: How do you read ة when you stop on it?
explain: Right.
That is for continuing.
That is how you stop on ـًا, not on ة.
Tanween's n drops when you stop.

questions.q: What does ta marbuta look like?
options: ه with two dots on top
explain: Right.
Three dots on that shape would be ث.
That is the shape of alif maqsura (ى).
That is not a letter shape used here.
Right.
A long 'ii' is a dotless ya after a kasra.
The consonant 'y' has its own vowel.

questions.q: In this mushaf, a final dotless ya comes after a kasra and has no mark of its own. How is it read?
explain: Right.
Long 'aa' needs a fatha before it.
A consonant 'y' has its own vowel.
It is a madd letter, so it is read.

questions.q: You stop on a word ending in ـةً (ta marbuta with tanween fath). How do you end?
explain: Right.
That is only for ـًا without ة.
'-tan' is for continuing.
Ta marbuta becomes 'h', not 't', at a stop.

questions.q: Which clue shows that a final ى is alif maqsura (a long 'aa')?
options: A fatha before it, often with a small alif on it (ىٰ)
explain: Right.
After a kasra it is a long 'ii'.
With dots it is a ya.
Alif maqsura carries no sukun.

questions.q: How is ه different from ة?
options: ه is always 'h'; ة is 't' unless you stop
ه is silent at the end of a word
explain: Right.
They are different letters.
ه is always pronounced.
Only when you stop on it.

options: Only at the end of a word
explain: Right.
It never starts a word.
It is limited to the end.

questions.q: A dotless final ى carries its own fatha (ـىَ). How is it read?
explain: Right: it has its own vowel, so it is a consonant.
Alif maqsura has no vowel of its own.
A long 'ii' has no vowel of its own.
It is pronounced.

questions.q: You continue past a ta marbuta with a damma (ـةُ). What do you say?
explain: Right.
'h' is only for stopping.
When continuing it is a 't', not an 'h'.
There is no long vowel here.

questions.q: Why must you look at the vowel before a final ى in this mushaf?
options: Because ى can be 'aa', 'ii' or 'y' depending on it
Because the vowel before it is always a fatha
explain: Right.
It is read in all three cases.
It is a real letter.
A kasra or its own vowel are common too.

questions.q: In Hafs, how do you stop on the few words the mushaf spells with an open ت where you might expect ة?
options: You may not stop on them
explain: Right.
'h' is for words written with ة.
There is no alif to lengthen.
Stopping on them is allowed.

remnote: Ta marbuta (ة) == 't' with its vowel when you read on; 'h' (ـهْ) when you stop
Alif maqsura (ى after a fatha, often ىٰ) == Long 'aa', 2 counts
Dotless final ى after a kasra == Long 'ii'
